claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in single-phase HEAs increases local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances hardness and yield strength.
The baseline material is a homogeneous, single-phase HEA with relatively low atomic size mismatch.
Compositional substitution or addition of an element with a substantially different atomic radius can increase atomic size mismatch.
Grain size, phase distribution, and other microstructural attributes should be held constant when comparing the modified alloy with the baseline.
Mechanical tests should be conducted at room temperature under identical processing and heat-treatment conditions.
Atomic size mismatch parameters can quantify the enhanced local lattice distortions.
Greater lattice distortion creates stronger local stress fields.
These local stress fields interact with and pin moving dislocations.
Dislocation pinning raises the energy required for plastic deformation.
The modified alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in hardness and yield strength relative to the lower-mismatch baseline.
The predicted increases in hardness and yield strength are caused by more pronounced inhibition of dislocation motion.
Beyond some threshold atomic size mismatch, phase segregation or second-phase formation may occur.
Phase segregation or second-phase formation would invalidate a direct attribution of strengthening to single-phase lattice distortion.
Local chemical ordering and processing-induced defects may also affect dislocation mobility and the magnitude of hardening.
TEM and XRD can be used to assess phase homogeneity and microstructural comparability.
Atomic pair-distribution-function analysis can be used to quantify lattice distortion.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength in the higher-mismatch alloy would falsify the proposed strengthening relationship under the controlled conditions.

contradictions.description: The boundary treats phase separation or second-phase formation as a condition that invalidates the intended single-phase comparison, whereas the falsification rule treats the same occurrence as falsifying the lattice-distortion hypothesis. Such an occurrence is a confound or out-of-domain result, not a decisive falsification of the hypothesis within its stated boundary.
